newsitem.title: HONG KONG: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - New World Infra in market.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - New World Infra in market.

text.p: Hong Kong's New World Infrastructure launched its large loan into a quiet Asian debt market on Tuesday.

The size of the revolving credit/term loan facility was increased to US$600 million from US$500 million following oversubscription in the underwriting stage, coordinating arrangers HSBC Investment Bank Asia and Goldman Sachs (Asia) announced.
The deal pays an interest margin of 85 basis points and has a five-year tenor with bullet repayment at maturity.
New World Infrastructure is a subsidiary of New World Development Co and is principally engaged in infrastructure development projects in Hong Kong and China.
In addition to the coordination arrangers, 11 banks have joined the facility as arrangers and lead managers.
Details emerged on a US$100 million floating rate note launched for Indonesia's Mulia Industrindo Finance by Bank Bira.

The notes are guaranteed by PT Muliakeramik Indahraya and PT Mulia Industrindo. They pay a coupon of 153 basis points over the London Interbank Offered Rate and an all-in return of 170 basis points to top-tier participants.
Looking at other Indonesian credits, bankers said Bank Ekspor Impor Indonesia's Singapore branch is seeking US$100 to Us$200 million in new financing.
The Cayman Islands branch of the bank recently signed a US$45 million floating rate certificate of deposit issue.
The Philippines' Metropolitan Bank and Trust has mandated Deutsche Morgan Grenfell to arrange a US$140 million FRCD issue.

Philippine bank shares have been hit recently on fears that the banks may have extended large loans to the country's real estate sector. Property stocks have wilted amid worries that the sector may face the same pressures as Thai property companies.
Philippine President Fidel Ramos today tried to allay such fears, saying that the local property market was not about to crash.
"We feel there are enough safeguards in our laws to prevent a further decline or collapse (in the property sector) as feared by some analysts," Ramos told a news conference.
